title: Biopsychosocial predictive factors for developing chronic postsurgical pain after hip replacement surgery: A systematic review
authors: Rachel J.H. Smits; Rosa Poppen; Jetze Visser; Kris C.P. Vissers; Selina E.I. van der Wal
pain_condition_detail: chronic postsurgical pain after total hip arthroplasty for end stage osteoarthritis
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the biopsychosocial model as an organizing principle to structure the review of predictive factors into biological, psychological, and socioeconomic categories. It lists factors within each domain but does not define the model or specify cross-domain mechanisms. Integration is limited to mentioning multiple domains in the same narrative.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper notes that the association between neuropathic-like pain and CPSP disappeared after adjusting for central sensitization and pain catastrophizing, suggesting shared variance but no mechanism is specified. Socio-economic disadvantages are theorized to affect coping strategies and social support, but no pathway is detailed.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses the biopsychosocial label to structure the review but does not define the model or specify how domains interact
conceptual_tensions_2: Social factors are acknowledged as important but only one study reported on education, leaving the social domain largely unexamined
conceptual_tensions_3: The paper lists multiple risk factors in parallel without proposing a mechanism for how they combine or interact
additional_observations_1: The paper's primary contribution is a systematic catalog of predictive factors for CPSP after THA, organized by BPS domains, but it does not integrate the domains beyond listing them
additional_observations_2: The paper uses the term 'biopsychosocial' in the abstract, methods, discussion, and conclusion, but never defines what the model means or how it should be operationalized
additional_observations_3: The paper acknowledges the complexity of CPSP but does not propose a testable model or pathway linking the identified factors
synthesis_note: This systematic review uses the biopsychosocial model as an organizing principle to catalog predictive factors for chronic postsurgical pain after hip replacement. It provides a thorough list of biological and psychological factors but minimal social content. The domains are listed in parallel with no cross-domain mechanisms proposed, making it a multifactorial rather than integrative use of the BPS model.
coding_rationale: Typology is multifactorial because all three domains are present but treated in parallel. Triadic integration is 'none' because no three-domain mechanism or narrative is proposed. Social domain is 'minimal' because only education and race are briefly mentioned. The paper uses BPS language extensively but does not define or integrate the model.

title: Biopsychosocial predictive factors for developing chronic postsurgical pain after hip replacement surgery: A systematic review
authors: Rachel J.H. Smits; Rosa Poppen; Jetze Visser; Kris C.P. Vissers; Selina E.I. van der Wal
pain_condition_detail: Chronic postsurgical pain after total hip arthroplasty for end-stage osteoarthritis.
context_note: Worldwide increase in total hip arthroplasties; no country-specific healthcare-system context reported.
bps_function_set: conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; operational definition; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The review operationalizes BPS through eligibility and extraction of preoperative patient-related biopsychosocial/economic predictors, then organizes results into biological, socioeconomic, and psychological sections. It uses BPS to justify prehabilitation, multimodal analgesia, and informed consent, but does not define the model or specify cross-domain mechanisms.
integration_mechanism_summary: No detailed cross-domain mechanism is proposed. The paper asserts directional links, notes possible coping/social-support mechanisms, and reports that neuropathic-like pain associations may be explained by central sensitization and catastrophizing.
quality_assessment_tools_3: grading of recommendations assessment, development and evaluation (grade)
emergent_labels_10: Quadratus lumborum of Pericapsular Nerve Group block
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses a broad BPS frame while not defining the model itself
conceptual_tensions_2: Biological and psychological evidence is detailed, but socioeconomic evidence rests mainly on one education study
conceptual_tensions_3: Pain sensitization, neuropathic-like pain, and catastrophizing overlap, and adjustment changes associations
conceptual_tensions_4: Many reported associations are inconsistent across observational studies
conceptual_tensions_5: Clinical implications extend to preoperative opioid reduction and digital adherence support even though some were excluded or not included
additional_observations_1: Meta-analysis was not conducted because of heterogeneity and limited studies per category
additional_observations_2: All included studies were observational cohort designs, resulting in low overall quality
additional_observations_3: The review distinguishes modifiable from non-modifiable risk factors for prehabilitation and informed consent
additional_observations_4: Some included studies also included knee or shoulder arthroplasty but required separate THA data
additional_observations_5: The paper uses 'biopsychosocial' to organize risk-factor extraction and clinical recommendations rather than to define variables in a single predictive model
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS as a structured inventory of preoperative predictors for CPSP after THA. Biological and psychological factors are developed in detail; socioeconomic factors are mentioned but evidence is thin; lifestyle implications are added in discussion. It proposes no cross-domain mechanism and mostly links domains as associated risk factors.
coding_rationale: BPS is primarily an organizing/intervention frame. Bio and psych are elaborated, social and lifestyle mentioned, spiritual absent. Triadic integration is descriptive, not mechanistic.

citation: Smits et al. (2026), Osteoarthritis and Cartilage Open
title: Biopsychosocial predictive factors for developing chronic postsurgical pain after hip replacement surgery: A systematic review
authors: Rachel J.H. Smits; Rosa Poppen; Jetze Visser; Kris C.P. Vissers; Selina E.I. van der Wal
pain_condition_detail: chronic postsurgical pain after total hip arthroplasty for end-stage osteoarthritis
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: Organizes risk factors into biological, psychological, and socioeconomic domains without specifying integration mechanisms between them.
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS labeling and minimal social domain coverage
conceptual_tensions_2: Inconsistent findings across studies for same risk factors
conceptual_tensions_3: Lack of integration mechanisms despite BPS framing
additional_observations_1: Review focuses on modifiable risk factors for prehabilitation and optimization
additional_observations_2: Uses GRADE approach for evidence quality assessment
additional_observations_3: Includes both biological and psychological measures but limited social measures
synthesis_note: This systematic review identifies multiple biopsychosocial risk factors for chronic postsurgical pain after total hip arthroplasty. It uses the biopsychosocial label as an organizing principle to categorize risk factors across biological, psychological, and social domains. However, the review does not specify integration mechanisms between domains, representing a multifactorial rather than integrative approach. The biological and psychological domains are elaborately covered with specific constructs and measures, while the social domain is minimally addressed. The review's strength lies in its comprehensive identification of risk factors for clinical application, but it lacks theoretical
coding_rationale: BPS typology as 'multifactorial' because all three domains are present but lack integration mechanisms. Domain coverage: biological and psychological elaborated, social mentioned. Integration rated 'none' due to absence of cross-domain pathways.
biological_factors_01_factor_verbatim: Eight studies reported on the association between age and chronic pain after THA. One study demonstrated a rise in pain of 0.18 on a 0–100 scale for each additional year in age.
biological_factors_02_factor_verbatim: One study reported that women experienced more pain 12 months post-surgery, with a mean increase of 2 points on a 0–100 scale.
biological_factors_03_factor_verbatim: Eight studies included Body Mass Index (BMI). One study reported significantly higher BMI in patients with a Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) pain score >3 (mean BMI 30.8) at 6 months postoperatively compared to those with a NRS <3 (mean BMI 27.4).
biological_factors_04_factor_verbatim: One study linked tobacco use to bothersome pain at six months but not to high-impact pain.
biological_factors_05_factor_verbatim: Two studies identified neuropathic-like pain as a prognostic factor for CPSP after THA... One study used as score of ≥13 on the modified painDETECT questionnaire (mPDQ) to discriminate between nociceptive pain and neuropathic-like symptoms. Preoperative neuropathic-like symptoms was linked to moderate and severe pain.
biological_factors_06_subdomain_label: Sensory Phenotype and Quantitative Sensory Testing
biological_factors_06_factor_verbatim: Preoperative pain sensitization was studied in three studies. Widespread pain sensitivity was measured by assessment of forearm pain pressure threshold (PPT) at the pain free volar forearm. Lower PPT indicates a higher pain sensitivity, and was strongly associated with CPSP after 12 months in one study.
biological_factors_07_factor_verbatim: The third study used the Central Sensitization Inventory (CSI), for identifying central sensitization symptoms. A score of 40 or more was an independent risk factor for CPSP 12 months after THA, with a NRS >3.
biological_factors_08_factor_verbatim: One study assessed disability with a subscale of the Western Ontario and McMaster Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC), with a higher score indicating more disability. Patients were allocated in three clusters, based on pain intensity, interference and disability. They found a significant association between disability and cluster 2.
biological_factors_09_factor_verbatim: Three studies mentioned comorbidity. One study used the Deyo-Charlson score which consists of a weighted scale of 17 comorbidities and uses the outcome of this score as a continuous variable for their analyses.
psychological_concepts_01_definition_ver: One study found that poor sleep quality, with a score of >5 on the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI, 0–21), was significantly associated with CPSP at 6 months postoperatively.
psychological_concepts_02_concept_family: depression, low mood and negative affect
psychological_concepts_02_definition_ver: Three studies linked depressive symptoms to CPSP at 6 months... A higher preoperative score on the Center for Epidemiological Studies-Depression scale was a predictor in one study.
psychological_concepts_03_definition_ver: Six studies evaluated anxiety. Preoperative anxiety (DASS) was associated with CPSPS at 6 months in one study. A trait anxiety score >46 was a risk factor for pain with an intensity of >30/100 after 1 year in another study.
psychological_concepts_04_definition_ver: Preoperative pain catastrophizing was assessed using the Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS) in three studies. One study found that a PCS ≥19/52 is a significant predictor for CPSP at 12 months.
psychological_concepts_05_definition_ver: Preoperative pain sensitization was studied in three studies. Widespread pain sensitivity was measured by assessment of forearm pain pressure threshold (PPT) at the pain free volar forearm. Lower PPT indicates a higher pain sensitivity, and was strongly associated with CPSP after 12 months in one study.
social_factors_01_factor_verbatim: Patients who do not identify as White were more likely to develop high impact and bothersome CPSP at 6 months compared to White patients, in one study.
social_factors_02_factor_verbatim: One study briefly mentions education. When using the baseline characteristics, a univariate analysis found no significant effect of the education level on CPSP at 6 months.
